0.body: Nix tooling to enable declarative management of non-volatile system state. Inspired and heavily influenced by impermanence but not meant to be a drop-in replacement.
0.title: Keep

10.body:
Specify multiple persistent storage locations to preserve state at. Each attribute name is the path of a persistent storage root; the entry’s dirs and files are stored beneath it. Entries are independent: they may serve different users and apply different settings. Type: attribute set of (submodule) Default: { } Example: { keepTo."/keep/host_systems" = { # system-level, paths are absolute (username defaults to "root") enable = true; dirs = ["/var/lib/service"]; }; keepTo."/keep/user_data" = { # paths are relative to the user's home dir enable = true; username = "alice"; dirs = ["Documents"]; };
} Declared by: options.nix
10.title: keepTo

11.body:
Specify a list of dirs that should be preserved. The paths are interpreted as absolute paths for system entries (when username is root), or relative to the user’s home dir when username is set to another user. Type: list of ((submodule) or string convertible to it) Default: [ ] Example: [ "/var/lib/someservice"
] Declared by: options.nix
11.title: keepTo.<name>.dirs

3.body: This aims to provide a declarative state management solution for NixOS systems without resorting to interpreters to do the heavy lifting. This should enable impermanence-like state management on an "interpreter-less" NixOS system.

41.title: keepTo.<name>.hideMount

42.body: Specify the user for which dirs and files are preserved. The default root configures system-level preservation: paths are interpreted as absolute paths and ownership defaults to root. When set to any other user, paths are interpreted relative to that user’s home dir (home), and parent dirs on persistent storage are configured with the user’s ownership and permissions. Multiple entries with different users may be configured side by side, each under its own attribute name (path). Type: string, not containing newlines or colons Default: "root" Example: "alice" Declared by: options.nix
42.title: keepTo.<name>.username

47.body: Impermanence is the established solution for managing persistent state on NixOS systems. Keep is inspired and heavily influenced by impermanence. See Comparison for a high-level overview of their differences.
47.title: Impermanence

48.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Comparison » How does Keep compare to impermanence
48.title: How does Keep compare to impermanence

49.body: Keep tries to fill a specific niche. For instance, Keep does not support non-NixOS systems via home-manager, which is supported by impermanence. See Migration for more technical details.
49.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Comparison » Keep does not attempt to be a very generic solution
49.title: Keep does not attempt to be a very generic solution

5.body: Each keepTo."<path>" entry supports: username: the user whose state is preserved. Defaults to root, i.e. system-level preservation with absolute paths. Any other user interprets dirs and files relative to that user's home dir and defaults ownership to that user. hideMount: adds the mount options x-gvfs-hide and x-gdu.hide to every bind-mounted entry of this location. dirs / files: the paths to preserve. Plain strings are accepted and coerced.
5.title: Storage location options

50.body: That is configuration for systemd-tmpfiles and systemd mount units . This makes Keep a potential candidate for state management on interpreter-less NixOS systems. Impermanence makes use of NixOS activation scripts and custom systemd services with bash (at the point of writing this), to create files and dirs, setup mounts and configure ownership and permissions (see next point).
50.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Comparison » Keep only generates static configuration
50.title: Keep only generates static configuration

51.body: There is no special runtime logic in place. This means that the user must define: when the preservation should be set up: either in the initrd, or after (the default) how the preservation should be set up: either by symlink, or bindmount (the default) whether or not parent dirs of the persisted files require special permissions See Migration for specifics that need to be considered when coming from an impermanence setup.
51.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Comparison » Keep must be precisely configured
51.title: Keep must be precisely configured

52.body: Keep's configuration is based on, and very similar to that of impermanence. See Migration for technical details.
52.title: Similar configuration

53.body: The keep module does not use an enable switch: an entry is active as soon as it has something to preserve, i.e. its dirs or files are non-empty. This differs from both impermanence and upstream preservation. To disable an entry whose lists are populated by other modules, override them with empty lists (lib.mkForce []). For thoughts on the enable option, see the discussion at https://github.com/nix-community/impermanence/pull/171 and for available configuration options see Configuration Options .
53.title: No enable option

54.body: Impermanence provides a hideMounts option, which sets the mount option x-gvfs-hide for bind-mounts. The keep module provides a similar hideMount option, which adds x-gvfs-hide and x-gdu.hide to the mount options of every bind-mounted entry. Additionally, keep allows for the configuration of arbitrary mount options per file and dir via mountOptions.
54.title: Generic hideMount option

55.body: This section lists individual differences between impermanence and Keep, to better understand them in context of a complete configuration Examples may be helpful. The following points need to be considered when migrating an existing impermanence configuration to Keep:
55.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Migration » Migration from impermanence to Keep
55.title: Migration from impermanence to Keep

56.body:
An entry under keepTo."<path>" is active as soon as its dirs or files lists are non-empty. There is no separate enable option. To disable an entry whose lists are populated by other modules, override them with empty lists: keepTo."/state" = { dirs = lib.mkForce []; files = lib.mkForce [];
};
56.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Migration » No global enable switch
56.title: No global enable switch

57.body:
Coming from a setup with impermanence it is important to make sure existing persistent state is preserved correctly, meaning the ownership and mode of preservation remains the same. There is no exhaustive list of files and dirs requiring special treatment but at least the following needs to be considered: SSH host keys Correct ownership and mode of SSH host keys is very important for sshd to accept connections. Getting this wrong, e.g. not restricted enough, may cause your host to become inaccessible via SSH, forcing you to use other means of logging into the machine. The following config may be used to preserve the RSA and Ed25519 host keys with Keep: keepTo."/state".files = [ { file = "/etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key"; method = "symlink"; parent.enable = true; } { file = "/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key"; method = "symlink"; parent.enable = true; }
]; The above config does not include access modes for the key files because the preservation mode is symlink and the link's target is not touched by preservation without an explicit mkTarget = true. Secrets and other files requiring special access modes Any files and dirs that need to have a mode that differs from the default (0644 for files and 0755 for dirs) must be configured explicitly to avoid having the default mode applied.
57.breadcrumbs: Impermanence » Migration » Handling of existing state
57.title: Handling of existing state

58.body:
Files and dirs that need to be persisted early, must be explicitly configured. For example /etc/machine-id: This file needs to be persisted very early, by explicitly setting inInitrd to true: keepTo."/state".files = [ { file = "/etc/machine-id"; inInitrd = true; }
];
58.title: When to persist

59.body:
The mode of preservation must be set explicitly for some files and dirs. This can be done by setting method to either symlink or bindmount (default). For most cases the default is sufficient but sometimes a symlink may be needed, for example /var/lib/systemd/random-seed. This file is expected to not exist before it is initialized. A symlink can be used to cause its creation to happen on the persistent volume: keepTo."/state".files = [ { file = "/var/lib/systemd/random-seed"; # create a symlink on the volatile volume method = "symlink"; # prepare the preservation early during startup inInitrd = true; }
]; Note that no file is created at the symlink's target, unless mkTarget is set to true.
59.title: How to persist

6.body: Every entry in dirs and files additionally accepts: method: how the path is preserved, either bindmount (the default) or symlink. user, group, mode: ownership and permissions on both volumes. parent: ownership and permissions of the path's parent dir (enable, user, group, mode). mkTarget: with method = "symlink", create an empty dir/file as the symlink's target on the persistent volume. inInitrd: prepare the preservation already in the initrd. mountOptions: additional mount options, only used for bindmounts.
